title: “WHEN YOU PASS THROUGH THE WATERS, I WILL BE WITH YOU” — NOTICE GOD NEVER SAID YOU WOULD AVOID THE WATERS
paragraphs: “WHEN YOU PASS THROUGH THE WATERS, I WILL BE WITH YOU” — NOTICE GOD NEVER SAID YOU WOULD AVOID THE WATERS
Maybe the water around you is not proof that God abandoned you. Maybe you have misunderstood what His promise was supposed to look like.
There is a sentence in Scripture that sounds beautiful until life forces you to need it.
Not quote it.
Not post it.
Not underline it.
Need it.
“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee…” — Isaiah 43:2.
Read that again, but this time notice the words we often hurry past.
When you pass through the waters.
Not if.
Not “I will make certain you never see deep water.”
Not “Follow Me faithfully enough and I will keep every river away from you.”
God never promised that.
And perhaps that is why somebody reading this has been quietly wondering whether God has forgotten them.
Because the water came.
You prayed.
And it still came.
You believed.
And it still came.
You tried to obey God, and somehow you still ended up standing in a place you never imagined you would have to survive.
The diagnosis came.
The marriage cracked.
The person you trusted betrayed you.
The child you prayed for wandered.
The business collapsed.
The bills kept arriving.
The grief stayed longer than everyone expected.
The temptation you thought you had defeated came knocking again.
The secret struggle followed you into another year.
You smiled at church while something inside you was drowning.
And somewhere between all the prayers that seemed unanswered and all the nights nobody knew you cried, a terrifying question entered your heart:
“God… if You are really with me, why am I in this water?”
That question deserves more than a Christian cliché.
It deserves Scripture.
And Scripture gives us something far stronger than the promise of an easy life.
The Hebrew of Isaiah 43:2 begins:
כִּי־תַעֲבֹר בַּמַּיִם אִתְּךָ־אָנִי
Ki-ta'avor bammayim, itt'kha ani.
“When you pass through the waters, I am with you.”
Look closely at the heart of it:
אִתְּךָ־אָנִי — itt'kha ani — “I am with you.”
That is the promise.
Not the absence of water.
The presence of God.
And that changes everything.

Isaiah was speaking first into the story of Jacob—Israel—a people God had created, formed, called, and redeemed. The verse was not originally written as a motivational slogan promising that every modern believer will escape every earthly disaster unharmed.
The context is richer than that.
Listen to what comes immediately before the waters:
אַל־תִּירָא כִּי גְאַלְתִּיךָ קָרָאתִי בְשִׁמְךָ לִי־אָתָּה
Al-tira, ki ge'altikha; qarati v'shimkha; li-attah.
“Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.” — Isaiah 43:1.
Before God talks about the river, He talks about belonging.
Before He describes the fire, He reminds His people who they are.
Before He tells them what they will walk through, He tells them whose they are.
“I have redeemed you.”
“I have called you by name.”
“You are Mine.”
Then comes the water.
That order matters.
Because suffering has a way of making you forget your identity.
Pain starts whispering things God never said.
“If God loved you, this wouldn't have happened.”
“If you had more faith, you wouldn't be struggling.”
“Maybe God is punishing you.”
“Maybe you went too far.”
“Maybe everybody else can be restored, but not you.”
“Maybe your scandal is bigger than His grace.”
And suddenly the river outside of you becomes a river inside of you.
Fear.
Shame.
Regret.
Anger.
Confusion.
You begin interpreting God through your circumstances instead of interpreting your circumstances through what God has revealed about Himself.
But Isaiah 43 turns the question around.
God does not begin by explaining the water.
He begins by declaring ownership.
You are Mine.
Somebody needs to hear that tonight.
You may be crying…
but if you are in Christ, your tears do not cancel His grace.
You may be struggling…
but your struggle does not make Jesus stop being Savior.
You may have fallen…
but failure does not suddenly make the cross powerless.

You may have consequences to face. You may need to repent. You may need to confess what you have hidden, make something right, seek forgiveness, receive help, or walk through a long process of restoration.
Grace is not pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is the staggering truth that sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and God's mercy is so great that sinners who come to Christ in repentance and faith can be forgiven.
That is why the Gospel is not the story of good people being rewarded for staying dry.
It is the story of guilty people being rescued by a holy and merciful Savior.
And this is where Isaiah's language becomes even more beautiful.
The word translated “redeemed” in Isaiah 43:1 comes from the Hebrew root גאל — ga'al.
It carries the language of redemption—the action of reclaiming or delivering.
God identifies Himself as the One who redeems.
And for the Christian, that great biblical story of redemption reaches its center in Jesus Christ.
We were not merely people caught in unfortunate circumstances who needed encouragement.
Our deepest problem was deeper than anxiety, deeper than financial pressure, deeper than rejection, deeper even than death.
We were sinners who needed reconciliation with God.
And Jesus did not stand safely on heaven's shoreline shouting instructions at drowning people.
He entered our world.
He took flesh.
He was rejected.
He suffered.
He was crucified.
And He bore sin so that those who trust in Him could be forgiven and brought to God.
Jesus knows what suffering costs.
The Christian faith does not give us a Savior untouched by pain.
It gives us the crucified Christ.
Think about that the next time your suffering whispers, “God could never understand this.”
Look at the cross.
The hands pierced there belong to the One Christians confess as Lord.
And then remember something else.
The cross was not the end.
The tomb was occupied…
and then it wasn't.
Jesus rose.
So Christianity does not promise that believers will never enter darkness.
It announces that darkness does not get the final word.
It does not promise there will never be a Friday that feels like everything has died.
It declares that because Christ is risen, death itself will not have the last word over those who belong to Him.
This is why you must be careful about judging God's faithfulness by the chapter you are currently living.
You are reading one page.
God sees the story.
You see water.
He sees a road through it.
You see fire.
He sees what will remain when the flames have done everything they are permitted to do.
You see an ending.
God may be writing a testimony.
And sometimes…
the miracle is not that the water disappears.
Sometimes the miracle is that you discover you are still standing in water that should have destroyed you.
You lost something and thought you would never smile again.
But one morning, somehow, you did.
You were betrayed and thought you would never trust again.
But God slowly began rebuilding your heart.
You buried someone and wondered how the world could possibly keep moving.
Yet grace met you one morning at a time.
You fell into sin and believed your story was permanently stained.
Then repentance brought you back to the feet of Jesus.
You thought your scandal would become your identity.
Jesus called you by another name.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
His.
That does not mean every earthly story gets the ending we want.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Some wounds leave scars.
Some relationships are not restored.
Some consequences remain even after forgiveness.
Some believers have followed Christ faithfully and still endured persecution, poverty, sickness, grief, and death.
The Bible never hides this.
Jesus Himself said, “In the world ye shall have tribulation.”
But He did not stop there.
“Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Hope.
Not pretending the fire isn't hot.
Knowing the fire isn't God.
Not claiming the river isn't deep.
Knowing the river isn't Lord.
Not pretending death doesn't hurt.
Knowing death does not have the final victory.
And perhaps that is what somebody needs tonight.
You have spent months asking God to remove the water.
Maybe tonight your prayer becomes different.
“Jesus, if You do not remove it yet… walk with me through it.”
That prayer is not surrender to defeat.
It is surrender to God.
There are seasons when faith sounds like thunder.
And there are seasons when faith barely whispers:
“Jesus… I still trust You.”
Do not despise the whisper.
A trembling hand can still reach for Christ.
A tired believer can still pray.
A wounded heart can still repent.
A person with tears running down their face can still worship.
You do not have to pretend you are okay to come to Jesus.
You simply have to come.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Maybe everybody knows the polished version of you.
They know your Sunday clothes.
Your Bible verses.
Your worship songs.
Your “God is good” posts.
But they do not know what happens when the phone goes dark and the room becomes quiet.
They don't know about the addiction.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The affair.
The resentment.
The secret messages.
The envy.
The anger.
The compromise.
The loneliness.
The shame.
The exhausting performance of looking spiritually alive while feeling spiritually numb.
And maybe your deepest water is not something somebody did to you.
Maybe it is something you did.
Listen carefully.
Grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace calls you into the light.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become more comfortable with chains.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Restore.
Transform.
So repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you become worthy.
You will never make yourself worthy of grace.
Come now.
Confess the sin.
Turn from it.
Call upon Christ.
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Stop protecting the secret that is poisoning your soul.
Stop assuming that because people might reject you, Jesus therefore must reject every sinner who comes to Him.
The Gospel exists precisely because sinners need mercy.
This is what makes grace scandalous.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted Christians.
The woman at the well carried a complicated past.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left with which to build an impressive religious résumé.
Again and again Scripture confronts us with people whose stories looked disqualified.
Then grace entered the story.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and then points trembling sinners toward a Savior whose mercy is greater than anything they could earn.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let sin have the final word over the repentant sinner who belongs to Him.
Maybe your life does not look like the testimony you imagined.
Maybe you thought by this age you would be farther ahead.
Maybe you thought your marriage would be stronger.
Your children closer to God.
Your finances stable.
Your faith fearless.
Your prayers answered.
Your heart healed.
Instead, you are standing waist-deep in something you never planned for.
Then hear the promise again.
Not the promise you wish the verse made.
The promise it actually makes.
כִּי־תַעֲבֹר בַּמַּיִם אִתְּךָ־אָנִי
“When you pass through the waters, I will be with you.”
Notice one more word.
Through.
The water is real.
But it is not necessarily your address forever.
There is a difference between passing through something and belonging to it.
You may be walking through grief.
Grief does not own you.
You may be walking through temptation.
Temptation does not own you.
You may be walking through consequences.
Your worst decision does not have to become your eternal identity.
You may be walking through a season where you cannot understand God.
Your confusion does not dethrone Him.
And if you belong to Christ, even death itself becomes something the believer passes through on the way to resurrection.
That is how deep Christian hope goes.
Not “everything will become comfortable.”
Something infinitely greater:
Christ will have the final word.
So if this found you while you are in the water, stop measuring God's nearness by how dry your clothes are.
He never said you would avoid every river.
He said:
I will be with you.
And maybe years from now, you will look back at the season you begged God to erase and realize it became the place where you finally stopped knowing Him merely as information…
and began knowing Him as refuge.
Maybe you will remember the night you nearly gave up.
The night you finally confessed.
The night you stopped running.
The night you whispered the name of Jesus because you had nothing eloquent left to pray.
Maybe the testimony will not be:
“I never entered the water.”
Maybe it will be:
“I entered it convinced I would drown… and discovered Christ was there.”
If that is where you are right now, don't hide behind a polished comment.
Be honest.
Somebody reading beneath you may be standing where you once stood.
Your testimony might become somebody else's reason to hold on tonight.
Then think of one person whose water is rising.
Not twenty random people.
One person.
The friend whose smile has been hiding exhaustion.
The brother who stopped coming to church.
The sister carrying a grief she rarely mentions.
The person whose marriage is quietly breaking.
The believer who thinks falling means Jesus wants nothing more to do with them.
The skeptic who has mistaken Christianity for a promise of an easy life.
Send this to them privately.
“Where is God in this?”
Let the answer find them:
He never promised there would be no waters. He promised His presence in them.

Save the truth for the night the water rises again.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done for you.
Because the mission is not to build an audience around us.
The mission is to point people toward Him.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
Calling people out of darkness.
Calling the guilty to repentance.
Calling the ashamed toward grace.
Calling the exhausted to Himself.
Calling prodigals home.
And perhaps that is why you are reading this at this exact moment.
You wanted God to explain the water.
Instead, Scripture gives you something better than an explanation.
A presence.
“I will be with you.”
So when the river rises tomorrow…
when another bill arrives…
when the memories return…
when temptation whispers…
when grief sits beside you again…
when people misunderstand you…
when repentance costs you something…
when the future becomes frightening…
remember what God did not say.
He did not say you would never see water.
And remember what He did say.
אִתְּךָ־אָנִי
I am with you.
The water may become part of your testimony.
But it does not get to become your Savior.
Jesus already has that name.
And when grace has finished telling your story, the chapter you once called “the place where I drowned” may become the chapter where you whisper through tears:
“That was the place I discovered I was never walking alone.”
Never confuse deep water with an absent God—the scars on the risen Christ remind us that suffering and the presence of God were never opposites.
